vignette:
He remembers the night as though it were yesterday, though it happened seven years ago. He had just finished a long day of sales calls across three counties, pulling into a motel just off the interstate. The parking lot was nearly empty. He was tired, thinking only of a shower and the stack of receipts he still had to organize. As he stepped out of his car, a man appeared from between two trucks, asking for money. Before he could respond-before he could even reach for his wallet-the man struck him across the face with something hard, then again on the side of his head. He fell. The man kicked him twice in the ribs and once in the back, then grabbed his briefcase and ran. The entire thing lasted maybe forty seconds.

He lay there for a long time, unable to move, waiting for someone to come. No one did. Eventually he pulled himself up, drove himself to a hospital three towns away, and told the nurse he had tripped. He never filed a police report. He told his wife it was a mugging-a brief, frightening moment-and then he tried to put it behind him.

But he could not put it behind him.

Now, at seventy, he still sells-office supplies, mostly, to mid-sized companies in the region. He has done it for forty-two years. His territory is the same, but his willingness to travel has shrunk. He insists on driving only during daylight hours, and he avoids the interstate altogether, taking longer back roads that remind him of his childhood. If a client meeting runs late, feeling pressure to stay for dinner, he becomes restless, his hands clammy, his mind fixed on the drive home. The thought of arriving at a motel-any motel-makes his stomach tighten. Two years ago he started lying to his manager, saying his wife was ill, just to avoid overnight trips. The lie still works. His manager has not questioned it.

At home, his wife notices the changes. He no longer enjoys the dinners out they once shared. Crowded restaurants make him anxious; he scans the room constantly, looking for exits. He prefers to sit with his back to a wall, and if someone approaches his table from behind, he flinches. She has learned to touch his shoulder gently, warning him before she speaks. Their conversations have become shorter. He often says he is fine, then retreats to the garage to tinker with old fishing gear he never uses.

He has not told anyone about the nightmares. They happen three or four times a month: the same motel, the same shadow, the same blow to the face. He wakes up breathless, his heart pounding, convinced someone is in the bedroom. He gets up, checks every lock, looks out the window, then lies back down, still and quiet, waiting for dawn. His wife sleeps through it; he does not want to worry her.

Work itself has become a performance. He can still charm clients, still close a deal, but the effort exhausts him. Small talk feels hollow. He finds himself replaying the assault during long drives, wondering what he could have done differently. He knows it is irrational, yet the thought loops repeat. Sometimes, when a customer is impatient or raises his voice, he feels a surge of adrenaline so strong he has to excuse himself to the restroom and breathe slowly until his hands stop trembling.

He told his therapist last week that he is not anxious. He said it with a flat smile. Then he described the way he now parks his car-facing out, always.
